name: Imperial Japanese Army and Navy doctrine (1941-1945)

weightNotes.aggression: 'The Japanese seem to feel that there is some mystic virtue in the attack'; officers chose to attack even where orthodox tactics demanded defence (TM-E 30-480 ch. VII). Every infantry manual 1909-1945 stressed the offensive (Drea, Nomonhan, ch. 1).
weightNotes.maneuver: Sokusen sokketsu: short, decisive war by encirclement using mobility, night movement and concentration (Drea, Nomonhan). Malaya 1941-42 was fast infiltration down the peninsula; island battles later were static. Moderately high.
weightNotes.flanking: 'The envelopment is the preferred form of attack'; the Japanese tried double envelopments even without numerical superiority, and sent small forces round to the enemy rear (TM-E 30-480 ch. VII).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Took fortresses and bases when they were the objective (Hong Kong, Singapore, Bataan and Corregidor), but doctrine aimed at the enemy force. Low-moderate.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Advance guards took a third to a half of a division's infantry and units were committed in full (TM-E 30-480 ch. VII); piecemeal commitment on Guadalcanal. Low.
weightNotes.scouting: Good pre-war intelligence for Malaya, but chronic underestimation of the enemy: Ichiki's detachment of about 900 attacked a Marine division on Guadalcanal, and late carrier scouting contributed to Midway. Low-moderate.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.worldwars high quartile 0.355, consistent with the shares at withdrawal on Guadalcanal: Edson's Ridge 1942, about 830 of some 3,000 attackers lost in the attack before Kawaguchi withdrew, about 28% killed alone (Edson's Ridge page); Henderson Field 1942, 2,200-3,000 killed of 20,000 before Hyakutake called off the attacks, 11-15% (Henderson Field page). Previous 0.95 came from Iwo Jima and Attu totals (99%), which include weeks of mopping-up after organised resistance ended; garrisons that could not withdraw are not a withdrawal share. Sourced refusal to surrender or retreat (TM-E 30-480; Drea) puts the doctrine at the top quartile.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Training stressed 'infantry tactics as opposed to combined arms tactics' and spiritual training to compensate for weak artillery and armour (Drea, Nomonhan). Naval aviation was strong, which keeps it above the floor.
weightNotes.initiative: Commanders and staffs operated well forward and junior officers were aggressive (TM-E 30-480 ch. VII); offset by rigid adherence to complex plans (Midway) and insubordination at the top (Kwantung Army).
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Operations routinely outran supply: Guadalcanal ('Starvation Island'), Imphal 1944 where troops were expected to live on captured stores, New Guinea. Very low.

summary: An infantry army and a carrier navy built for a short, decisive war. The army relied on surprise, envelopment, night attack and the spirit of the offensive to compensate for weak artillery, armour and industry; commanders attacked even against superior forces and treated defence as a temporary state. The navy built a powerful carrier striking force and trained intensively for night surface combat with long-range torpedoes. Logistics was an afterthought. From 1944 the army switched to fortified defence in depth on islands (caves and bunkers on Peleliu, Iwo Jima, Okinawa) designed to bleed the attacker, still ending in suicidal counterattacks.
whyItWorked: Against unprepared colonial garrisons in 1941-42 speed, surprise and infiltration were overwhelming: Pearl Harbor, the Philippines, Malaya and Singapore (February 1942) fell within months. Night actions such as Savo Island (August 1942) showed the navy's training edge. The 1944-45 island defences inflicted very heavy US casualties (Iwo Jima, Okinawa).
whereItFailed: Nomonhan 1939, where Soviet combined arms crushed infantry spirit; Midway, June 1942, four fleet carriers lost through poor scouting and an over-complex plan; Guadalcanal, August 1942 to February 1943, where piecemeal night attacks (Tenaru, Bloody Ridge) broke on prepared Marine positions and starvation and disease killed more men than combat; Imphal-Kohima 1944, an offensive launched without supply that cost most of the Fifteenth Army; banzai charges at Attu and Saipan; Leyte Gulf, October 1944.
